title: Susan's three blocks
source: School paper (Nan Hua Primary School, WA3 2025, Q1)
stem:
Susan placed three blocks, R, S and T, into a container of water. Her observation is shown below.

She made the following statements:

A Only block T does not absorb water.
B Blocks S and T are made of different materials.
C Blocks R and S are made of the same materials.

Which statement(s) can be concluded from her observation?
figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 520 220" role="img" aria-label="A container of water with blocks: R rests on the bottom; S rests on the bottom; T floats at the surface."><rect x="22" y="78" width="476" height="124" style="fill:var(--fa);fill-opacity:.55;stroke:none"/><path class="ln" d="M22 20 V202 H498 V20"/><path class="ln" d="M22 78 H498"/><rect class="sl" x="70" y="152" width="84" height="50" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="112" y="183" text-anchor="middle">R</text><rect class="sl" x="190" y="152" width="84" height="50" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="232" y="183" text-anchor="middle">S</text><rect class="sl" x="330" y="56" width="84" height="44" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="372" y="84" text-anchor="middle">T</text></svg>
hints: Ask of each statement: does the picture show it, or is it only something that might be true?
One test only shows that blocks behave differently, or that they behave the same.
key: Different results prove different materials. Matching results prove nothing. The float test says nothing about absorbing water.

options.text: B only
options.pick: Reach it by comparing S and T: S sinks and T floats in the same water, so they behave differently.
options.why: S sinks and T floats. A different result on the same test means they are made of different materials. A and C go further than the picture allows.

options.text: B and C only
options.pick: B is right, and R and S look alike because both sit on the bottom.
options.why: R and S both sank, but different materials can both sink. A matching result does not show the same material, so C cannot be concluded.

options.text: A and C only
options.pick: T is the only block at the surface, so it seems the only one that is not soaking up water. R and S sink together, so they seem alike.
options.why: Floating or sinking does not show whether a block absorbs water: that needs the mass before and after soaking, so A cannot be concluded. C cannot be concluded either, and B, which can, is left out.

options.text: A, B and C
options.pick: Every statement seems to match something in the picture.
options.why: Only B can be concluded. A needs a mass measurement and C needs more than one matching result.

title: Three blocks, three tests
stem:
Mei Ling tested three blocks, X, Y and Z, in the same way. The results are shown.

Which of the following can be concluded from the results?
figure:
BlockIn waterWhen bentMass before soaking (g)Mass after soaking (g)
Xsinksbreaks5050
Ysinksbreaks6080
Zfloatsbends without breaking4070
hints: Find a test where the two blocks in the statement gave different results.
For absorbing water, work out mass after − mass before.
key: One different result is enough to prove two blocks are different materials. Matching results never prove they are the same.

options.text: X and Y are made of the same material because they both sink and both break when bent.
options.pick: Two of the three tests match, so X and Y seem alike.
options.why: They also differ in the soaking test: X absorbed 0 g and Y absorbed 20 g. One different result proves they are different materials.

options.text: Y and Z are made of the same material because they both absorbed water.
options.pick: Both masses went up after soaking.
options.why: Y sinks and Z floats, and Y breaks while Z bends. Both absorbing water does not make them the same material.

options.text: X and Y are made of different materials.
options.pick: Look for a test where X and Y differ: X absorbed 0 g (50 − 50) but Y absorbed 20 g (80 − 60).
options.why: The soaking results are different, so X and Y cannot be the same material, even though they match on floating and bending.

options.text: Z does not absorb water because it floats.
options.pick: Floating blocks stay on the surface, so they seem to stay dry.
options.why: Z absorbed 70 − 40 = 30 g of water, even though it floats. Floating does not show that a block is waterproof.

title: The block that floats
stem:
Ravi put a block into a container of water. The block floated at the surface. Its mass was 80 g before soaking. After it stayed in the water for 10 minutes, its mass was 95 g.

Which of the following can be concluded?
hints: Float or sink is one test. Mass before and after soaking is a different test.
Work out mass after − mass before.
key: Floating and absorbing water are two separate properties. A block can float and still absorb water.

options.text: The block is waterproof because it floats.
options.pick: Waterproof sounds like staying on top of the water.
options.why: The mass went up by 15 g, so the block absorbed water. Waterproof means it does not absorb water, and floating does not show that.

options.text: The block floats, and it also absorbed water.
options.pick: Combine the two results: it floated, and 95 − 80 = 15 g of water went in.
options.why: The float test and the soaking test are separate, and both results are in the stem.

options.text: The block floats because it absorbed water.
options.pick: The block took in water and also floats, so one seems to cause the other.
options.why: Nothing in the results shows that absorbing water makes a block float. They are two separate results.

options.text: The block is waterproof because its mass changed by only 15 g.
options.pick: 15 g is a small change compared with 80 g.
options.why: Waterproof means the mass does not change at all. A gain of 15 g means the block absorbed water.

title: Kumar's blocks E, F and G
stem:
Kumar put three blocks, E, F and G, into a container of water. His observation is shown below.

He made the following statements:

A Blocks E and F are made of the same material.
B Blocks F and G are made of different materials.
C Block G does not absorb water.

Which statement(s) can be concluded from his observation?
figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 520 220" role="img" aria-label="A container of water with blocks: E floats at the surface; F floats at the surface; G rests on the bottom."><rect x="22" y="78" width="476" height="124" style="fill:var(--fa);fill-opacity:.55;stroke:none"/><path class="ln" d="M22 20 V202 H498 V20"/><path class="ln" d="M22 78 H498"/><rect class="sl" x="70" y="56" width="84" height="44" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="112" y="84" text-anchor="middle">E</text><rect class="sl" x="190" y="56" width="84" height="44" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="232" y="84" text-anchor="middle">F</text><rect class="sl" x="330" y="152" width="84" height="50" rx="2"/><text class="lbl" x="372" y="183" text-anchor="middle">G</text></svg>
hints: Which statement compares two blocks that gave different results?
Which statements stretch one result too far?
key: A different result proves different materials. A matching result, and the float test alone, prove nothing more.

options.text: A and B only
options.pick: E and F both float, so they seem the same. F and G differ, so B is right.
options.why: B is right. A is not: E and F both floating does not show they are the same material.

options.text: B and C only
options.pick: B is right. G sinks, so it seems to be the block that is not soaking up water.
options.why: B is right. C is not: sinking says nothing about absorbing water.

options.text: A and C only
options.pick: E and F match, and G seems to sit dry on the bottom.
options.why: Neither A nor C can be concluded, and B, which can, is left out.

options.text: B only
options.pick: F floats and G sinks in the same water, so they are made of different materials.
options.why: Different results prove different materials. A (matching results) and C (float test only) cannot be concluded.

title: A fair test for floating
stem:
Hui Min wants to find out if the type of material affects whether a block floats. She has blocks made of wood, glass and metal, and a large container of water.

Which row shows what she should change and what she should keep the same?
hints: The thing you want to find out the effect of is the one you change.
Whether the block floats is what you observe.
key: Change only the thing you are testing (the type of material). Keep everything else the same. What you observe is the result.

options.pick: The blocks go into water, so water seems to be what changes.
options.why: The question is about the type of material, so that is what she changes. The type of material cannot be the thing kept the same.

text: amount of water and size of the blocks
options.pick: The type of material is what she is testing; everything else is kept the same so only the material can affect the result.
options.why: Only the type of material changes, so any difference in floating can be put down to the material.

text: whether the block floats or sinks
options.pick: The blocks float or sink differently, so it seems to be what changes.
options.why: Whether it floats is the result she observes. It is not set by her.

options.pick: Blocks come in different sizes, so size seems like the thing to change.
options.why: If the size changes and the material is kept the same, she is testing size, not material.

title: Marble, nail and duck
stem:
Wei Jie put three objects into a container of water. A glass marble sank. A steel nail sank. A plastic toy duck floated.

Which of the following can be concluded?
key: Different results prove different materials. Matching results prove nothing.

options.text: The marble and the nail are made of the same material because both sank.
options.pick: They behave the same way in the water.
options.why: Two different materials can both sink. A matching result does not show the same material.

options.text: The marble and the duck are made of different materials.
options.pick: The marble sank and the duck floated: a different result.
options.why: Different results in the same test show different materials.

options.text: The duck does not absorb water.
options.pick: It stays on the surface.
options.why: Floating does not show whether an object absorbs water. That needs the mass before and after soaking.

options.text: The duck floats because it is light.
options.pick: Small, light things seem to float.
options.why: Nothing in the results shows this. Whether an object floats depends on what it is made of, not how light it is.

title: Torch and three blocks
stem:
Aisha shone a torch through three blocks, M, N and O, one at a time. Block M let most light through. Block N let no light through. Block O let no light through.

Which of the following can be concluded?
key: Different results prove different materials. Matching results prove nothing.

options.text: Blocks M and N are made of different materials.
options.pick: M and N gave different results with the torch.
options.why: Different results mean different materials.

options.text: Blocks N and O are made of the same material.
options.pick: N and O gave the same result.
options.why: A matching result does not show the same material. Different materials can both let no light through.

options.text: Block O lets more light through than block M.
options.pick: The torch result seems to point to O.
options.why: M let most light through and O let none, so it is the other way round.

options.text: Block M is waterproof.
options.pick: Light-passing materials such as glass seem waterproof.
options.why: The torch test says nothing about water, so this cannot be concluded.
